item.title: A1 · Can People Still Afford Rent? Then vs Now
item.description:
1. Three yardsticks, not one. The rent burden (Mietbelastung) is gross cold rent, meaning the basic rent plus the service charges paid to the landlord but not heating, as a share of household net income. Social scientists and property experts usually treat a burden above 30 percent as problematic, a rule of thumb rather than a measured boundary. The overburden rate used by Eurostat and the OECD counts people in households that spend more than 40 percent of disposable income on housing; in its wider version, housing costs also include utilities, maintenance and taxes. The third yardstick is residual income: what is left after housing costs, compared with the subsistence minimum. One research paper on German rent burdens puts it plainly: affordability cannot be measured directly, so rent-to-income ratios serve as a measurable indicator.
2. The official snapshot for 2022. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), tenant households spent on average 27.9 percent of their net income on gross cold rent, at 8.60 euros per square metre. In the first results, about 3.1 million households, 16 percent of tenant households, paid 40 percent or more. There is a catch for any "then versus now" question. Since the 2020 redesign of the Mikrozensus, the household survey behind these numbers, Destatis says 2022 cannot be compared with earlier years.
3. The long-run trend: up, then flat. Using the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP), a household survey run since 1984, the DIW Berlin economists Konstantin Kholodilin and Pio Baake find that the burden rose in the early 1990s, has been roughly constant since about 2005, and has slipped slightly since 2015. In East Germany it jumped from about 4 percent in 1990 to about 25 percent in 2001, after rents frozen since 1936 were liberalised. Backhaus, Gebers and Schröder found the same shape: a substantial rise in the 1990s, then a relatively constant decade. Kholodilin and Baake name rising incomes, the rent brake (Mietpreisbremse, introduced in 2015 for new lettings in tight markets) and fewer moves as possible reasons for the recent slight fall, but say their data cannot show how much the brake mattered.
4. Rents against incomes. Asking rents, the rents advertised for new lettings, rose about 55 percent between 2010 and 2022, and about 70 percent in cities above 500,000 people. Rents in existing tenancies rose only about 19 percent. Over a shorter window, an Institut der deutschen Wirtschaft (IW) short report by Ralph Henger found that rents in multi-family buildings rose 10.2 percent from 2010 to 2016 while disposable household income rose 11.5 percent. Niklas Gohl, citing federal data, puts the rise for new contracts between 2010 and 2015 at about 18 percent nationally and 26 percent in big cities.
5. Sitting tenants versus newcomers. The federal research institute BBSR reports that in 2025 the average asking rent for a re-letting was 11.11 euros per square metre, against an estimated 7.76 euros for existing contracts: about 43 percent higher. Growth in asking rents slowed from 5.7 percent in 2023 to 4.8 and then 3.5 percent in 2024 and 2025. BBSR's explanation is that most flats are let long-term, and increases in running contracts are infrequent and legally limited. Gohl describes those limits as of 2019: a cap of 20 percent in three years, or 15 percent where states have designated tight markets. The size of the gap depends on the yardstick. BBSR's asking rents come from online adverts and its existing-rent figure is an estimate, while the IW found an average premium for new contracts of 14 percent in 2016 to 2018.
6. Newcomers: a third more per square metre, but a smaller gap in burden. In 2022 the average burden by move-in year was 26.9 percent before 1999, 27.3 percent for 1999 to 2008, 27.1 percent for 2009 to 2018, and 29.6 percent for 2019 or later. Recent movers pay 9.70 euros gross cold per square metre against 7.30 for pre-1999 tenants, about a third more, yet their burden is only about three points higher. The table does not say why. The IW reported that new tenants lived in somewhat less space per person than sitting tenants, 45.6 against 49.5 square metres in 2018.
7. Income is the sharpest divide. In 2022, households with under 1,500 euros net a month spent 44.6 percent of income on gross cold rent; households with 4,000 euros or more spent 15.9 percent. Households of four or more people under 1,500 euros spent 58.0 percent. Single-person households averaged 32.7 percent, two-person households 22.8 percent. Over time, Kholodilin and Baake find that the poorest fifth of tenants went from about 24 percent in 1990 to about 36 percent in 2021, while the richest fifth paid about 22 percent. Dustmann, Fitzenberger and Zimmermann, using a different survey and counting owners too, find that the bottom fifth's share of income spent on housing rose from 27 percent in 1993 to 39 percent in 2013, while the top fifth's fell from 16 to 14 percent.
8. Place matters, but less than income. In 2022 the burden was 29.0 percent in large cities, 27.7 percent in medium-sized towns and 26.0 percent in small towns and rural areas. Gross cold rent averaged 9.60 euros per square metre in large cities, and 11.00 euros for those who moved in from 2019. The burden for large-city newcomers was 30.9 percent. The spread by city size is far narrower than the spread by income. Asking rents in 2025 ranged from 21.01 euros in Munich to 8.64 in sparsely populated rural districts, and below 6 euros in parts of Saxony and Thuringia. Kholodilin and Baake find burdens lower in the East, with the statistical region of Chemnitz at 21.6 percent and the Cologne administrative district at 30.7 percent. The IW calculated, for new-contract rents, how much space a single median earner can rent for a quarter of net income: 36.2 square metres in Munich, 57.3 in Düsseldorf. Between 2018 and 2021, affordability fell in about three quarters of districts.
9. Germany in Europe: bad or good, depending on the yardstick. In 2025, 11.2 percent of Germany's population lived in households overburdened by housing costs, against 7.7 percent for the EU. The rate was 9.0 percent in 2020 and peaked at 13.0 percent in 2023; Destatis notes that figures from 2020 on are not comparable with earlier years because of a survey break, and that changed questions for owners in 2023 limit comparison with earlier years. Among people at risk of poverty the rate was 35.0 percent in 2025. Yet the OECD lists Germany among just five countries where fewer than half of low-income tenants in the private market are overburdened when total housing costs are counted. Germany also has the highest tenant share in the EU, with 52.8 percent of the population renting.
10. Residual income tells a related story. A Humboldt University team (Andrej Holm and colleagues), funded by the Hans-Böckler-Stiftung, used the 2018 Mikrozensus for 77 large cities. They found 12.9 percent of tenant households, about 1.1 million, had less than the subsistence minimum left after paying rent including utilities. The top income class had 4.4 times the net income of the bottom class before rent, and 6.7 times after it. A study of Berlin, Cologne and the Ruhr area from 2002 to 2018 by Marco Schmandt points the other way in aggregate: residual income rose along the whole distribution in two of the three markets despite real rent increases, largely because of changes in who lives there (abstract only).
